evidence.label: Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem for one transformation

headline: If long waits make any two moments independent, they make every finite group of moments independent.
scope: The main theorem covers one invertible, probability-preserving, mixing transformation, with every gap between times growing.
plain: A mixing system forgets its past: what happens now and what happens much later become independent. A question traced to Rokhlin in 1949 asks whether this forces three or more far-apart moments to be independent too. Pairs can be independent while triples are linked, so the answer was not obvious. This paper proves the answer is yes for every invertible mixing transformation, and a proof checker has checked it. No extra structure on the system is needed.
doesNot: This does not cover systems with two independent directions of time. Ledrappier's 1978 example shows those can fail.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: V. A. Rokhlin, higher-order mixing and the question
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it answers Rokhlin's 1949 question for one transformation with no extra structure assumed.

explanation:
Flip two fair coins and write 1 for heads, 0 for tails. Call the results X and Y. Now set a third digit Z. It is 1 when X and Y differ, and 0 when they match. Four outcomes are equally likely: 000, 011, 101 and 110. Each digit is 1 half the time. Each pair of digits is 1 together a quarter of the time. That is exactly ½ × ½, so any two digits look independent. Yet all three digits are never 1 together. Full independence would predict 1 time in 8.

That gap between pairs and triples sits at the heart of a question from 1949. The question is about a rule T that moves the points of a space, step by step. Picture stirring a drink. The rule is probability-preserving: it never shrinks or swells the share of space a region takes up. It is invertible: every step can be undone. The rule is mixing when long waits erase memory. Take two regions, A and B. Count the points that start in A and sit in B after n steps. As n grows, their share tends to the share of A times the share of B. If A and B each fill half the space, that share tends to ¼.

Mixing of order 3 asks the same for three regions visited at three times, with both gaps growing. Then the share should tend to the product of three shares, such as ⅛ for three halves. Mixing of order k asks it for k regions. V. A. Rokhlin introduced these higher orders in 1949. Thierry de la Rue presents his 1949 question as this: does ordinary mixing alone imply the next order? The coin example shows why the answer is not automatic. Pairs can be independent while a triple stays linked.

With two independent directions of time, the answer is no. In 1978, F. Ledrappier gave a mixing example on a grid that is not mixing of order 3. In 2006, de la Rue explained why a direct one-dimensional copy of it fails. Positive answers for one rule needed extra structure. S. A. Kalikow showed in 1984 that order 2 gives order 3 for one special class. B. Host in 1991 and V. V. Ryzhikov in 1993 reached all orders for other special classes. In 2024, A. Kanigowski and D. Ravotti did so for certain flows, which are motions in continuous time. A general mixing rule has none of that structure.

This paper proves the general answer is yes. Every invertible, probability-preserving, mixing rule is mixing of every finite order. It assumes no special form for the rule. It also imposes no technical regularity condition on the space.

The proof argues by contradiction. Suppose some order fails, and take the smallest one that does. Then every smaller group of times behaves independently, but the full group does not. That is the coin pattern again, and pairwise independence alone does not force full independence. The paper first trims the failure down to a very predictable process. Such a process has zero entropy: long stretches follow relatively few likely patterns. After that step, the new difficulty is to control every leftover interaction at once, not just one chosen snapshot. It then shows any hidden link must ride on special wave-like functions. These come in finite blocks that time shuffles as wholes. Averaging over time makes those links cancel. That contradicts a positive quantity that time preserves.

So no mixing rule can hide a coin-style link between three far-apart moments. With three half-size regions and all gaps long, the triple share must approach ⅛. The same holds for any number of regions. The statement is about limits only. It names no rate, so it does not say how long the gaps must be. It concerns one rule repeated in time, which is exactly where Ledrappier's grid example does not apply. The paper also extends the result to rules that cannot be undone, and to certain flows.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the main theorem. It covers every order from 3 up and every choice of measurable regions. The Lean scope note links it to a fixed reference statement for a checking tool called Comparator. The extensions to non-invertible rules and to flows are not in that scope note. No specialists have published a review yet.
hypeCheck: Landmark only if the proof holds. Lean has checked a formal version of the main theorem. The extensions to non-invertible maps and flows are outside the scope note. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A rule that moves points of a space without changing the share of space any region fills.
Every step of the rule can be undone by another rule of the same kind.
Being in one region now and in another after a long wait become independent events.
The same independence for k regions at k times, as all gaps between the times grow.
The chance of events happening together equals the product of their separate chances.
A motion that runs in continuous time instead of whole steps.
A tool that checks a Lean proof matches a fixed reference statement.
